query: For high-value components operating in aggressive environments, what intervention could improve surface physical and mechanical characteristics? Formulate one hypothesis specifying the intervention, its proposed mechanism, the expected improvement relative to an untreated baseline, the conditions under which it should remain effective, prior evidence that would support it, and an experiment whose outcome could falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Applying a thermal shock treatment (annealing at 800 °C for 1 hour) to an as-deposited AlCrTiZrMo high-entropy alloy film will induce the in situ formation of a dense composite oxide layer (primarily ZrTiO4) that significantly enhances both its surface physical integrity and mechanical resistance (reducing friction and wear) in aggressive environments compared to the untreated film.
generation.material_initial_state: As-deposited, strongly amorphous AlCrTiZrMo high-entropy alloy film prepared by a controlled deposition method (e.g., Co-FCVAD) with an unoptimized surface structure.
generation.intervention: Thermal shock treatment by annealing the film at 800 °C for 1 hour in air.
generation.conditions: Aggressive service environments such as high-temperature oxidation and tribocorrosion conditions (e.g., high-temperature sliding in corrosive media).
generation.structural_mediator: Formation of a dense, composite ZrTiO4 oxide layer on the film’s surface.
generation.mechanism: The rapid thermal annealing promotes elemental segregation and oxide formation at the film’s surface. The resultant dense and stable oxide layer acts as a barrier that hinders further oxidation and reduces mechanical damage during friction, thereby lowering wear and friction coefficients.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to the untreated film, the annealed film will exhibit lower open-circuit potential variance (ΔOCP), reduced coefficient of friction (COF), and a lower wear rate under identical tribocorrosion tests.
generation.baseline: The as-deposited AlCrTiZrMo HEA film without any post-annealing treatment.
generation.boundary: The enhanced properties are expected to be effective under conditions similar to those in the thermal shock and tribocorrosion tests (around 800 °C in air or similarly aggressive environments). The improvement may diminish if the film composition or deposition parameters change significantly.
generation.uncertainty: The quantitative extent of the improvement (e.g., exact percentage reduction in wear rate or COF) may vary with subtle differences in film microstructure and environmental specifics; additional tests are needed to generalize the behavior across different HEA compositions.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of identical AlCrTiZrMo HEA film samples via the same deposition process. Subject one set to annealing at 800 °C for 1 hour (thermal shock intervention) and leave the other set untreated. Then perform standardized tribocorrosion tests in a controlled high-temperature oxidative environment with consistent loading, sliding frequency, and electrolytic conditions.
measurements: Open Circuit Potential (OCP) variation (ΔOCP) during sliding
Wear rate calculated from wear volume, applied load, and sliding distance
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the thermal shock treated samples do not show statistically significant improvements (i.e., lower ΔOCP, reduced COF, and lower wear rate) compared to the untreated baseline under identical test conditions, then the hypothesis that thermal shock induces a beneficial oxide layer enhancing surface and mechanical properties is falsified.

cited_evidence.kind: web:3.4. Tribocorrosion Performance after Annealing in Air Environment
cited_evidence.text: From Figure 10, the OCP curves of the AlCrTiZrMo HEA film and the film annealed at 400 °C have similar changes with ΔOCP values of 0.453 and 0.461, respectively. During the rapid sliding, the two curves remain stable due to the dynamic balance between activation and passivation within the wear track [,]. Additionally, the two COFs are 0.13 and 0.09, respectively (Table 5). As shown in Figure 11a,b, many adhesions and furrows are found on the abrasion track of the AlCrTiZrMo HEA film and the film annealed for 400 °C. The dense microstructure of the AlCrTiZrMo HEA film after annealing at 600 °C and the increased H and E improve the resistance to external damage, resulting in a reduction in ΔOCP, COF and wear rate. The ΔOCP, COF and wear rate of the AlCrTiZrMo HEA film annealed at 800 °C are minimized to 0.055, 0.04 and 1.34 × 10−6 mm−3·N−1·m−1, respectively, and no obvious wear characteristics appear in the abrasion track, which means that the film is not destroyed.
